beats.narration_text: Aloha — this is Liam, in for Divyank. A generated quiz question can look perfectly fine and still test the wrong thing entirely — passing every review while measuring nothing the chapter promised to teach. Let's build the assessments properly, then go hunt for exactly that failure.

show.event: composer cold-opens, spark + 'Aloha, Liam' greeting settles

send arms, runningText plays
RESULT lines land in sequence

props.command: Walk me through generating real assessments from a chapter, then finding a generated question that quietly tests the wrong thing.
output: quizzes and flashcards exploit real memory findings
Bloom's levels are the word for what's wrong
the audit checks the question against its outcome, not in isolation

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: Quizzes aren't a formality bolted onto the end of a chapter. Being tested on material improves long-term memory more than re-reading it for the same amount of time — a real, replicated finding, not a study habit someone made up.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of students taking a computerized exam -- illustrative of the testing effect, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A1-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push across the exam room
serif label lands: 'a memory intervention, not a grade'

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: Cram it into one sitting, or spread it out. Massed study feels more efficient and forgets faster. Spaced study feels harder and sticks — which is exactly what Anki's scheduling algorithm, S-M-2, from 1987, is built to enforce automatically.

show.event: question card: 'massed, or spaced?'
two outcomes: massed / spaced

beats.act: Act II — The Word For What's Wrong
beats.narration_text: To catch a bad question, you need a word for exactly what's wrong with it. That word is a level — and there are six of them, stacked, each one demanding more than the last.

shot.prompt: real archival spiral-staircase photo -- illustrative of climbing cognitive levels, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A2-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push up the staircase
serif label lands: 'six levels, stacked'

beats.act: Act II — The Word For What's Wrong
beats.narration_text: The outcome says Apply. The question asks the reader to Remember a definition instead. It looks fine. It reads like a real quiz question. And it measures absolutely nothing the chapter promised to build.

show.event: question card: 'does the question match the outcome's level?'
two outcomes: matches / mismatch

data.question: Does the question match the outcome's level?

branches.label: Matches
branches.detail: tests at Apply, like the outcome demands

beats.act: Act III — Generate, Then Hunt the Failure
beats.narration_text: Here's a real question, generated live, in agent mode, from this very book's own Chapter 3 — and then actually audited against the outcome it was supposed to serve.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of a vintage pocket watch's mechanism -- illustrative of examining something closely, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A3-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the watch mechanism
serif label lands: 'a real question, actually audited'

beats.act: Act III — Generate, Then Hunt the Failure
beats.narration_text: The outcome demands Apply. The question tests Remember — a reader can pick the right answer from memory alone, without ever having built anything, without understanding why the build might actually break.

show.event: two tracks diverge: the outcome's demand arcs up, the question's actual level arcs down

tracks.label: The outcome
notes: produce an EPUB from a changed chapter

tracks.label: The question
notes: answerable from memory, never having built anything

beats.narration_text: Four specific ways this exercise fails — and every one of them traces back to skipping the audit, not to a bad generator.

shot.prompt: real archival railway-crossing warning sign photo -- illustrative of what goes wrong, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A4-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push onto the sign
serif label lands: 'skipping the audit, not a bad generator'

beats.narration_text: 'The audit found nothing' can mean two very different things. Either every question really is aligned — or you graded questions in isolation, never once checking them against the outcome they were supposed to serve.

show.event: question card: 'the audit found nothing — why?'
two outcomes: genuinely aligned / graded in isolation

resolver.label: Always check which one happened
resolver.detail: a clean report can mean the audit never ran

beats.narration_text: Your turn — here's the prompt, read it with me. 'Generate a quiz question for one of my own chapters or documents, then tell me: what Bloom's level does the outcome demand, what level does the question actually test, and if they don't match, rewrite the question at the right level.' Run it. Liam, in for Divyank.
